description: Team-proposed weight set, pending advisor review. Not validated against advisor or reviewer judgement: the values are the team's reading of the CUAD category definitions, checked only for sensible firing rates on the training answers and a non-degenerate rating spread on the validation contracts. docs/risk-weights-v2.md explains every value and lists the open questions. Severities use five tiers (None 0, Low 0.25, Medium 0.5, High 0.75, Critical 1.0) and every one of the 41 categories is listed. Tier arithmetic with these weights: a plain clause scores 0.6 x its tier (0, 0.15, 0.30, 0.45, 0.60), a full one-sidedness or magnitude signal adds 0.10, and contract context adds 0.20 x the sum of its matching rule adjustments. So a plain clause rates by its tier (None and Low -> Low, Medium and High -> Medium, Critical -> High); one full-strength quote signal lifts a Low-tier clause to Medium and a High-tier clause to High; a Medium-tier clause needs both quote signals plus a context rule to reach High. Values assume a neutral reviewer, not a specific party. Not legal advice.

severity_rationale.Document Name: None: identifies the document; creates no obligation.
severity_rationale.Parties: None: identifies who signed; creates no obligation.
severity_rationale.Agreement Date: None: a date for the record; creates no obligation.
severity_rationale.Effective Date: None: says when obligations start, not what they are.
severity_rationale.Expiration Date: Low: the length of the commitment; a very long fixed term is caught by the magnitude rule.
severity_rationale.Renewal Term: Medium: automatic renewal can lock a party in past the term it planned for.
severity_rationale.Notice Period To Terminate Renewal: Low: a calendar item to diarise; the lock-in risk is carried by Renewal Term.
severity_rationale.Governing Law: Low: matters mainly when the law or forum is unfamiliar, which the system cannot judge.
severity_rationale.Most Favored Nation: High: ties the seller's pricing to every other customer deal and invites audits and repricing claims.
severity_rationale.Non-Compete: High: restricts what business a party may do, often beyond the contract term.
severity_rationale.Exclusivity: High: shuts out other suppliers or customers, so the party depends on one counterparty.
severity_rationale.No-Solicit Of Customers: Medium: limits who a party may sell to; narrower than a non-compete.
severity_rationale.Competitive Restriction Exception: Low: a carve-out that softens a restriction; worth a read to confirm it is wide enough.
severity_rationale.No-Solicit Of Employees: Low: common, usually mutual and time-limited; a long period is caught by the magnitude rule.
severity_rationale.Non-Disparagement: Low: restricts statements about the counterparty; rarely carries money exposure.
severity_rationale.Termination For Convenience: Medium: the counterparty can walk away without cause, so revenue and investment are uncertain.
severity_rationale.Rofr/Rofo/Rofn: Medium: gives the counterparty first claim on future deals, which can chill or delay other buyers.
severity_rationale.Change Of Control: Medium: a merger or sale of the business can need consent or end the contract.
severity_rationale.Anti-Assignment: Low: a consent requirement found in most contracts; mainly matters in a transaction.
severity_rationale.Revenue/Profit Sharing: Medium: an ongoing payment obligation that is hard to verify and often audited.
severity_rationale.Price Restrictions: Medium: limits the ability to raise or lower prices as costs and markets move.
severity_rationale.Minimum Commitment: High: money is owed whether or not the goods or services are needed (take-or-pay).
severity_rationale.Volume Restriction: Medium: exceeding a usage threshold triggers fees or needs consent.
severity_rationale.Ip Ownership Assignment: High: a party permanently gives up ownership of intellectual property it creates.
severity_rationale.Joint Ip Ownership: Medium: shared ownership makes licensing and enforcement depend on the co-owner.
severity_rationale.License Grant: Low: a core commercial term present in most licensing deals; a perpetual or irrevocable grant is caught by scope phrases.
severity_rationale.Non-Transferable License: Low: limits flexibility in a transaction but is standard licensing practice.
severity_rationale.Affiliate License-Licensor: Low: widens which licensor-group IP is covered; mainly a scope question.
severity_rationale.Affiliate License-Licensee: Low: widens who may use the licence; mainly a scope question.
severity_rationale.Unlimited/All-You-Can-Eat-License: Medium: usage is uncapped, so the licensor cannot charge for growth.
severity_rationale.Irrevocable Or Perpetual License: Medium: the licence cannot be taken back, even if the relationship ends badly.
severity_rationale.Source Code Escrow: Low: mostly protective for the licensee; the licensor's risk is a broad release trigger.
severity_rationale.Post-Termination Services: Medium: obligations survive the end of the contract, including transition, payments or last-buy.
severity_rationale.Audit Rights: Low: an operational burden that is standard in commercial contracts.
severity_rationale.Uncapped Liability: Critical: exposure has no ceiling, so one breach can cost more than the contract is worth.
severity_rationale.Cap On Liability: Low: limits exposure for the protected party; it reduces recovery for the other side but is market standard.
severity_rationale.Liquidated Damages: High: a fixed payment for breach or early termination is owed without proving loss.
severity_rationale.Warranty Duration: Low: the length of warranty cover; a short window is caught by the magnitude rule.
severity_rationale.Insurance: Low: a compliance cost; it mainly protects the counterparty.
severity_rationale.Covenant Not To Sue: Medium: a party gives up the right to challenge IP or bring certain claims.
severity_rationale.Third Party Beneficiary: Medium: someone who did not sign the contract can enforce it.

cooccurrence_rules.rationale: Unlimited exposure with no insurance requirement leaves nothing behind the promise to pay.
With a cap elsewhere, uncapped wording is usually a carve-out for specific breaches, not unlimited exposure overall. Also hedges the classifier's known habit of labelling cap language as uncapped.
A liability cap usually bounds the total of any fixed damages.
Fixed damages with no overall cap can add up without limit.
A carve-out narrows the restriction (CUAD defines the exception for Non-Compete, Exclusivity and No-Solicit of Customers).
A carve-out narrows the exclusive dealing commitment.
A carve-out narrows which customers are off-limits.
Exclusive and obliged to buy a minimum: the party can neither go elsewhere nor buy less.
The same lock-in seen from the purchase obligation.
No way to exit early, so the minimum is owed for the whole term.
Automatic renewal with no exit for convenience means a missed notice window locks in another full term.
Together they mean a merger or sale of the business needs the counterparty's consent.

magnitude_rules.rationale: Up to 6 months is common; 3 years or more is long enough to be challenged as unreasonable.
12 months is the typical period; 3 years is unusually long.
12 months is the typical period; 3 years is unusually long.
A one-year exclusive is a manageable bet; five years ties the party to one counterparty for a business cycle.
Annual renewal is the norm; a renewal of five years or more is a long, easy-to-miss lock-in.
A 90-day transition is routine; two years of surviving obligations is a real continuing cost.
A short warranty or inspection window (90 days or less) leaves the buyer little time to find defects; a year is typical.
Initial terms up to 5 years are common in the training contracts; 10 years or more is a long fixed commitment.
30 days' notice to walk away leaves little time to replace the business; six months gives room to plan.
